_readme: Spiritual vocabulary: theological terms whose WORD a modern reader knows but whose
weight and original-language sense they may not. Unlike glossary-en.json (false
friends) these have no modern substitute, so there is no `m`: you cannot swap the word,
only explain it. `d` is a neutral, definitional note; `o` the Greek/Hebrew term in
transliteration. Notes stay non-adjudicating: where a meaning is contested across
traditions (faith, salvation, justification, propitiation) the note says so rather than
picking a side, per docs/KJV-ONLY-CLAIMS.md. Common terms render in the Spiritual-terms
block only (no inline markers, or faith at 254 hits would bury the false friends). The
few that are also unfamiliar WORDS carry `inline: true` so they still mark the text.

faith.d: Belief, trust and reliance. The Greek pistis spans intellectual assent, personal trust, and faithfulness or loyalty; which of these it centres on is understood differently across traditions.

grace.d: Favour freely given and unearned. The Greek charis also means a gift or an act of kindness.

mercy.d: Compassion or clemency, especially the withholding of deserved judgement. Behind it stand Greek eleos and Hebrew chesed, steadfast covenant love.

salvation.d: Deliverance, rescue, or being made whole and safe. Whether it is spoken of as a past event, a present process, or a future hope varies across traditions.

righteousness.d: Being right or just, and standing in a right relationship. The same root gives 'just' and 'justify'; Hebrew tsedaqah, Greek dikaiosyne.

love.d: Committed, self-giving love. The Greek agape is the word the KJV often renders 'charity'; it is distinct from friendship (philia) and desire (eros).

redemption.d: Buying back or ransoming, as a captive or slave was freed by a price. Greek apolytrosis; the Hebrew go'el is the kinsman who redeems.

atonement.d: Reconciliation, and the covering or removal of sin. Hebrew kaphar means to cover. In the KJV New Testament the word appears once, at Romans 5:11, for Greek katallage, reconciliation.

sanctification.d: Being set apart, or made holy. Greek hagiasmos, from the same root as 'holy' and 'saint'.

justification.d: Being acquitted or set right. From the same root as 'righteous'; whether it means to declare righteous or to make righteous is debated across traditions.

forgiveness.d: Pardon, or release from a debt or wrong. The Greek aphesis is literally a sending away or letting go.

propitiation.d: A sacrifice that deals with sin. Whether the Greek hilasmos stresses turning aside wrath (propitiation) or wiping away sin (expiation) has long been debated.

longsuffering.d: Patient forbearance; slowness to anger under provocation. Greek makrothumia, literally long-tempered.

lovingkindness.d: Steadfast, loyal covenant love. Coined by Coverdale to render Hebrew chesed, which has no single English word.

remission.d: Release or pardon, especially of sins or debts. The Greek aphesis is the same word elsewhere rendered 'forgiveness'.

reconciliation.d: The restoring of a broken relationship to peace. Greek katallage; the KJV also renders it 'atonement' at Romans 5:11.

sin.d: Missing the mark, or going astray. Greek hamartia is an archer's word for a shot that falls short; the KJV also uses iniquity, transgression and trespass for related ideas.

iniquity.d: Guilt, and the crookedness behind it. Hebrew avon carries the sense of being bent or twisted out of true.

transgression.d: The crossing of a set limit, or rebellion against a command. Hebrew pesha is nearer to revolt than to an accidental slip.

trespass.d: A false step or lapse, and the debt it leaves. Greek paraptoma, a falling aside from the way.

repent.d: To turn, changing mind and course. Of people, Greek metanoeo; of God (as at Genesis 6:6) the Hebrew nacham is better read as to relent or be grieved, not to admit a fault.

repentance.d: A change of mind and direction, more than regret. Greek metanoia is a turning of the whole outlook.

gospel.d: Good news. From Old English god-spell, good tidings, rendering Greek euangelion, the announcement of a great event.

covenant.d: A binding bond between parties, stronger than a contract. Hebrew berith; Greek diatheke also means a will or testament, which is why we say Old and New Testament.

holy.d: Set apart and distinct, belonging to God, rather than simply well-behaved. Hebrew qadosh, Greek hagios, the root of saint and sanctify.

holiness.d: The state of being set apart to God, from the same root as holy.

glory.d: Weight, worth and honour, and also visible splendour. Hebrew kabod is literally heaviness; Greek doxa is brightness and renown.

wrath.d: Settled opposition to wrong, a judicial anger rather than a loss of temper. Greek orge.

mediator.d: One who stands between two parties to bring them together. Greek mesites, a go-between or arbitrator.

christ.d: A title, not a surname: the Anointed One. Greek christos translates Hebrew mashiach, Messiah; kings, priests and prophets were set apart with oil.

soul.d: The living self, or life itself, not a ghost housed in a body. Hebrew nephesh is the whole living being; Greek psyche is the life or self.

resurrection.d: A rising of the body to life again, not merely the soul living on. Greek anastasis, a standing up again.

eternal.d: Of the age to come; unending. Greek aionios relates to aion, an age, so it can point to a kind of life as much as to endless time. The KJV also says 'everlasting'.

everlasting.d: Unending, of the age to come. Renders Greek aionios and Hebrew olam, which can reach to the far distant past or future. The same idea as 'eternal'.

heaven.d: The sky, and the dwelling of God. Hebrew shamayim is plural, the heavens, and covers both senses; Greek ouranos likewise. Matthew's 'kingdom of heaven' is the same as the 'kingdom of God' elsewhere.

hell.d: One English word for four different originals: Hebrew sheol and Greek hades, the realm of the dead or the grave, not in themselves a place of torment; Greek gehenna, the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, pictured as fiery final judgement; and once (2 Peter 2:4) tartaros, where fallen angels are held. Later versions often keep these distinct rather than merging them into one word.

paradise.d: A garden or park, and so the blessed abode. Greek paradeisos is a loanword from Persian for a walled garden; it names Eden in the Greek Old Testament and the place promised to the thief at Luke 23:43.

perdition.d: Ruin, loss or utter destruction. Greek apoleia; 'son of perdition' means one headed for ruin.
